newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl acts on tax as hopes of an SPD deal fade.
newsitem.headline: Kohl acts on tax as hopes of an SPD deal fade.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Tuesday forged ahead with his coalition's tax reform agenda despite dwindling hopes of reaching a deal with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).
Kohl's cabinet approved Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1999 tax bill, the second stage of a 30 billion mark ($17.6 billion) tax-cutting plan which, if passed, would take effect next year.
The tax bill will be submitted to parliament this Friday and Waigel said he was hopeful that legislation for both 1998 and 1999 will clear the Bundestag lower house before the summer recess.
"The government is right on schedule," Waigel told a news conference. "With this tax reform we will open the way to more growth and jobs."

But getting the tax measures through the Bundestag will be the easy part. Kohl's 14-year-old coalition faces a rough ride in the upper house of parliament -- controlled by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).

To avert a legislative logjam, the two sides have been holding on-off talks to keep tax out of the 1998 general election campaign. More discussions were due to be held on Wednesday, but hopes for an agreement were fading fast.
Kohl on Monday wrote in an open letter to SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine saying the talks "only made sense" if the SPD agreed to real tax cuts and an overhaul of the social security system.

Lafontaine responded on the eve of the meeting that Kohl had got things back to front. He demanded a jobs-boosting cut in occupational insurance charges from July 1 and called again on the government to explain how it would cover revenue shortfalls the SPD estimates at 56 billion marks.

Lafontaine said in the letter it was possible at the talks to agree to cut labour insurances charges from July, to slash the bottom rate of income tax, to increase child allowances and to cut the main corporate tax rate.
But neither side appeared ready to give ground, with the negotiating climate further poisoned by last-minute wrangling over where the talks were supposed to take place.
Lafontaine told reporters he thought the meeting would be the last to try and preempt the looming gridlock of parliament's legislative process.
Both he and Waigel said they expected to meet again in parliament's slow-moving mediation committee, which is expected to be held this autumn.

Presenting the tax bill, Waigel said the reform could cover a third of its initial cost by stimulating growth by up to half a percent a year and encouraging Germans to be more candid in filling out their tax returns.
Key points of the 400-page 1999 tax bill would be cuts in the lowest income tax rate to 15 from 26 percent. The top rate would fall to 39 percent from 53 -- a move opposed by the SPD.
The main corporation tax rate would fall to 35 percent from 47 percent now, with the cuts partly offset by the abolition of over 70 tax breaks.
Waigel said Bonn's current budget difficulties would not lead him to rework his sums on the tax reform's impact.

He reiterated his commitment to meeting the Maastricht treaty's deficit target of three percent of GDP this year to qualify for Europe's single currency, even though Germany's six leading economic institutes predicted a borrowing overshoot of up to 3.2 percent.

"We will hold to the criteria, they will not be loosened," he said. "We will make it, and if the economic institutes say that we will be around 3.2 percent, but can also achieve a 'point landing', then we will do it."

Official tax revenue estimates for 1997 due next month are expected to show a big shortfall thanks to a winter surge in unemployment, but Waigel said the gap would not much exceed the government's January forecast of eight billion marks.

He also did not rule out the possibility of imposing a freeze on state spending or accelerating privatisation to help contain borrowing. "We can use appropriate measures to achieve this when carrying out the budget," he said. ($ = 1.703 German Marks)
